subject: physics
title: Radioactive decay and nuclear radiation
key_idea: Unstable nuclei give out radiation in a random process called **radioactive decay**. Alpha, beta and gamma radiation differ in what they are, how far they travel and how strongly they ionise. Alpha is the most ionising and the least penetrating. Gamma is the opposite.

blocks.text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable. The nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable.

items.meaning: A random process in which an unstable nucleus gives out radiation.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays. It is measured in becquerel (Bq).
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector such as a Geiger-Müller tube.
The radiation always present around us, which a detector also counts.

blocks.text: A Geiger-Müller (GM) tube is attached to a counter. Each time radiation enters the tube, the counter adds one count.

blocks.label: Count rate
blocks.formula: count rate = number of counts ÷ time
where: count rate is in counts per second.
number of counts has no unit.

blocks.text: To find the count rate from the source alone, subtract the background count rate.

blocks.label: Corrected count rate
blocks.formula: corrected count rate = measured count rate - background count rate
where: All three rates are in counts per second.

diagram.alt: Calculate a corrected count rate from a number of counts, a time and the background.
diagram.question: A Geiger-Müller tube and counter records {c} counts in {t} seconds near a radioactive rock. The background count rate is {b} counts per second. Calculate the corrected count rate for the rock.
working: Corrected count rate = {answer} counts per second

items: Radioactive decay is random and gives out radiation from the nucleus.
Activity is measured in becquerel (Bq). Count rate is the counts each second.
Subtract the background count rate to find the count rate from the source.

sections.heading: Alpha, beta, gamma and neutron radiation

blocks.text: Four types of radiation may be emitted from an unstable nucleus. The properties you need are what each is, how far it penetrates and how strongly it ionises.

items.meaning: Able to knock electrons off atoms and turn them into ions.
How far the radiation passes through a material before it is stopped.

rows: Two neutrons and two protons, the same as a helium nucleus
A high-speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton
Less than alpha, more than gamma
Reduced by several cm of lead or thick concrete

items: Alpha is the least penetrating and the most ionising. Gamma is the most penetrating and the least ionising.
A neutron (n) can also be emitted from an unstable nucleus.
A positron (β⁺) is emitted by some nuclei. Alpha, beta (β⁻), positron and gamma radiation are all ionising.

items: Alpha: helium nucleus, +2, most ionising, stopped by paper, a few cm in air.
Beta: fast electron, -1, stopped by thin aluminium, up to about 1 m in air.
Gamma: electromagnetic radiation, no charge, least ionising, reduced by thick lead.

blocks.text: A Geiger-Müller tube detects radiation. Photographic film also detects it, because radiation darkens the film.
Comparing the count rates of two sources

items: Put each source near the front of the tube, one at a time, at the same distance.
Measure the count for the same time period for each source.
Measure the background count, and take it into account.
Repeat the readings and take averages.

items.text: Record the count with no source present.
Place the source near the detector and record the count.
A large drop in count rate shows that alpha is emitted.
A further drop shows that beta is emitted.
If the count is still above background, gamma is emitted. If it falls to background, there is no gamma.

items: To test the range in air, move the detector away in steps and record the count each time until it reaches the background value.
Alpha radiation is not detected beyond a few cm. Beta and gamma radiation are still detected further away.
The count rate is less than the activity because not all the radiation emitted is detected. It spreads out in all directions.
Use a GM tube with the same distance and the same time, and allow for background.
Paper stops alpha, thin aluminium stops beta and thick lead reduces gamma.
The count rate is less than the activity.

blocks.text: The best source for a job depends on how far its radiation travels and how ionising it is.

items: A smoke detector uses alpha radiation. Beta and gamma radiation would penetrate smoke, so no change in count rate would be detected.
Alpha radiation cannot pass through a plastic case. A beta source would be more hazardous in a smoke detector, because it is more penetrating and could pass through the case.
A tumour can be treated with an alpha source inside the body, because alpha has a short range and the source must be close. A gamma source can be outside the body, because gamma is penetrating.
A beta source implanted near cancer cells has a short range in tissue. This increases the chance of killing the cancer cells and decreases the risk to healthy cells.
A gamma or beta source injected into the body can be detected by a camera outside the body, because the radiation passes out through the skin.
Beta particles cannot penetrate a metal container, so they do not reach people outside it.
Outside the body, alpha is stopped by skin so the risk is low.
Inside the body (internal contamination), alpha is absorbed by living tissue and is highly ionising. It causes greater harm to cells, tissues and DNA.
Radiation increases the risk of cancer and mutation, so stand as far away as possible from a source.
Use alpha where a short range is needed and gamma where radiation must pass through material.
Alpha outside the body is low risk. Alpha inside the body is high risk.

checks.q: State what an alpha particle, a beta particle and a gamma ray are.
checks.a: An alpha particle is two protons and two neutrons, the same as a helium nucleus. A beta particle is a high-speed electron from the nucleus. A gamma ray is electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus.

checks.q: A counter records 1500 counts in 30 seconds. Calculate the count rate.
A source's count rate drops to the background level when a thin sheet of aluminium is placed in front of the detector. It was reduced when paper was added. What does the source emit?
checks.a: Alpha and beta radiation. The drop with paper shows alpha. The count falling to background with aluminium shows no gamma.

mistakes.wrong: A beta source in a smoke detector would be more hazardous because beta is more ionising.
mistakes.right: This is not allowed. Beta radiation is more hazardous because it is more penetrating, so it can pass through the case and irradiate people nearby.
The background is subtracted. 819 ÷ 60 = 13.65 per second, and 13.65 - 0.30 = 13.35 per second. Adding scores only 2 of the 3 marks.

mistakes.wrong: The count rate is the same as the activity of the sample.
mistakes.right: The count rate is less than the activity because not all the radiation emitted is detected. It spreads out in all directions.

mistakes.wrong: The teacher stood back to avoid being contaminated.
mistakes.right: References to contamination are ignored. Say that standing back reduces the radiation received, and that radiation increases the risk of cancer or mutation.

worked_example.question:
A teacher wanted to find out what nuclear radiation is emitted from a source.

The teacher placed different barriers between the source and a detector and recorded the count for 30 seconds after each barrier was put in place.

With no barrier the count was 985.
With paper (0.1 mm) the count was 149.
With aluminium (5.0 mm) the count was 0.
No count was recorded with lead.

Explain what nuclear radiation was emitted by the source.
answer_points: Some radiation is stopped by paper (the count fell from 985 to 149).
So the source emits alpha radiation.
Some radiation passes through paper but is stopped by aluminium.
So the source emits beta radiation (but does not emit gamma).
worked_example.tip: The second and fourth marks depend on the first and third. State the barrier effect before naming the radiation.

exam_phrases: alpha short range / low penetration
needs to be close to the tumour
gamma long range / high penetration
can get into the body from outside
keep source-detector distance the same
measure each count for the same time period
repeat readings and take average(s)
there is no aluminium to absorb β particles

mistakes.wrong: Alpha is used inside the body because it is more ionising than gamma.
mistakes.right: This earns only 1 mark by itself. Link alpha's short range to the source needing to be close to the tumour, and gamma's long range to it getting in from outside.

mistakes.wrong: Put the rock inside the Geiger-Müller tube.
mistakes.right: Not allowed. Put the rock in front of or near the tube, and keep the two rocks apart.

mistakes.wrong: Take the count for each rock for as long as is convenient.
mistakes.right: Measure each count for the same time period and keep the source-to-detector distance the same.

mistakes.wrong: Measure the distance beta particles travel until the reading drops.
mistakes.right: Continue until the reading reaches the background value or a constant value, after measuring the background without the source.

worked_example.question:
Some tumours inside the body can be treated by using either alpha radiation or gamma radiation.

Explain why the source of alpha radiation is usually inside the body but the source of gamma radiation can be outside the body.
answer_points: Alpha has a short range or low penetration.
So the source needs to be close to the tumour.
Gamma has a long range or high penetration.
So gamma can get into the body from outside, passing through the skin.
worked_example.tip: Saying alpha is highly ionising, or gamma weakly ionising, is accepted. But 'alpha is more ionising than gamma' scores only 1 mark by itself.

exam_phrases: One absorber placed between detector and isotope
Drop in count rate with cardboard indicates alpha
Drop in count rate with aluminium indicates beta
Drop in count rate with lead indicates gamma
as it is the most/more penetrating / can be detected outside the body
Beta particles cannot penetrate metal / container
alpha is less penetrating / more easily absorbed

mistakes.wrong: Gamma is the best radiation for the camera because it does not harm the body.
mistakes.right: Ideas about effects on the body are ignored. Say that gamma or beta is more penetrating, so it can be detected outside the body. Less or least ionising is also allowed.

mistakes.wrong: Show only gamma is emitted by putting paper in front of the detector.
mistakes.right: References to paper are ignored. Use a thin aluminium sheet that stops alpha and beta. If the reading is the same with and without it, only gamma is emitted.

mistakes.wrong: The metal container stops the particles.
mistakes.right: Particles unqualified is ignored. Say that beta particles cannot penetrate the metal container, so they do not reach the technicians.

mistakes.wrong: Alpha radiation is always safer than beta radiation.
mistakes.right: Yes if you say alpha is less penetrating so cannot get through the skin. No if you say alpha is more ionising and causes more damage to cells inside the body.

worked_example.question:
Scientist 1 wants to identify the type of radiation emitted by isotope A.

This is a list of equipment Scientist 1 has in his laboratory:
• radiation detector
• piece of thick lead
• piece of cardboard
• piece of aluminium.

Describe how Scientist 1 does the experiment and explain how they can work out the type of radiation emitted.

You may include a diagram in your answer.
answer_points: Place one absorber between the detector and isotope A, then change the absorber and repeat (maximum two marks for the method).
Measure the background count with no source (also credited).
A drop in count rate with the cardboard indicates alpha.
A drop in count rate with the aluminium indicates beta.
A drop with the lead, or all the materials being penetrated, indicates gamma (maximum two marks for the conclusions).
worked_example.tip: Up to two marks for the method and up to two for linking drops in count rate to radiation. Stopped or absorbed is accepted for a drop in count rate.
